claims.text: Set the cable handles at about the top of the head, grasp one in each hand and stand in a staggered (walking) stance with the trunk upright.

quotes.text: Position the cable handles approximately level with the top of your head and grasp each handle firmly.
Assume a staggered-stance position (i.e., walking position, with one leg forward) to stabilize yourself and align your trunk vertically.

claims.text: Brace the abdominal muscles and avoid arching the low back throughout.

quotes.text: Stiffen (“brace”) your abdominal muscles to stabilize your spine, and attempt to avoid any arching of your low back throughout the exercise.

claims.text: Keep a slight bend in the elbows, the wrists straight in line with the forearms and the trunk vertical for the whole movement.

quotes.text: Maintain a slight bend in your elbows, neutral wrist position (i.e., wrists aligned in a straight line with your forearms)
Maintain the slight bend in your elbows, neutral wrist position and vertical alignment of your trunk throughout the movement.

claims.text: On the way back the arms open upward and outward, but the hands should not travel back past the level of the armpits.

quotes.text: Allow your arms to slowly open , moving upward and outward to your sides.
do not allow your hands to move past the midline of your body (level of your armpit).

claims.text: Squeeze the chest to sweep the arms forward and down until the hands meet below chest level, pause briefly, then return slowly.

quotes.text: Exhale gently and slowly squeeze your chest muscles to pull your arms forward until your hands meet below the level of your chest.
Pause momentarily then slowly return to your starting position, allowing your arms to move back outwards in a slow, controlled manner.

claims.text: Think of the arms moving downward first and then inward, in a wide arc (bent-forward cable crossover tip; applied here by inference).

quotes.text: Think about moving the arms downward first and then inward to get a nice wide arc.

claims.text: Leaning forward is a frequent fault, usually when the weight is too heavy; it raises the stress in the shoulder joint. The fix is a lighter weight and an upright trunk.

quotes.text: Avoid the tendency to lean forward during this exercise as this increases the stresses within the shoulder joint, which happens frequently when the resistance used is too heavy.
To protect your shoulders from potential injury, lower the resistance, align your trunk vertically and follow the instructions provided.

claims.text: Starting with the arms behind the torso, or crossing the handles past the midline, adds little and carries a risk of shoulder injury and of hurting the hands as the handles pass close together (bent-forward cable crossover tip; applied here by inference).

quotes.text: some exercisers start with the shoulders in horizontal hyperextension or the arms behind the torso, and then actually cross the two handles above and below each other to come past the midline.
quotes.where: Bent-forward cable crossover tip (Mark P. Kelly)

quotes.text: While this extreme range of motion may feel good, it does little in terms of muscular conditioning, and there is a risk of injury in the shoulder during hyperextension and of the hand when the handles pass so close to each other.
quotes.where: Bent-forward cable crossover tip (Mark P. Kelly)

claims.text: Don't move the torso toward the hands (bent-forward cable crossover tip; applied here by inference).

quotes.text: Avoid moving the torso closer to the hands,
quotes.where: Bent-forward cable crossover tip (Mark P. Kelly)

claims.text: The chest works strongly in cable crossovers: 93% of barbell bench press chest activation in an ACE-funded EMG study (bent-forward cable crossover; applied here by inference); ACE lists the decline cable fly's target as the chest.

quotes.text: Both the pec deck (at 98% of muscle activation compared to barbell bench press) and the bent-forward cable crossover (93% of muscle activation) elicited nearly equivalent muscle activation as the barbell bench press.
Target Body Part: Chest

claims.text: Inferred from other exercises, not measured on this fly: flyes (horizontal adductions) rank highest for front deltoid activation, while a declined bench press used the front deltoid less than flat or incline pressing. So the front deltoid helps, probably less than on flat or incline flyes.

quotes.text: For anterior deltoid, horizontal adductions (inclined) and horizontal adductions (horizontal) generated the greatest activation
Anterior deltoid was less excited (d: 3.84/19.77) in DBP compared to all other exercises.

claims.text: Tempo: ACSM's moderate 1-2 s each way (for heavy sets in trained lifters) gives up 2 and down 2. ACE asks to pause momentarily where the hands meet, right after the sweep, and gives no seconds, so the 1 s pause is a drawing convention (LR-33).

quotes.text: For intermediate (individuals with approximately 6 months of consistent RT experience) to advanced (individuals with years of RT experience) training
with eventual emphasis on heavy loading (1-6 RM) using 3- to 5-min rest periods between sets performed at a moderate contraction velocity (1-2 s CON; 1-2 s ECC)
Pause momentarily then slowly return to your starting position

claims.text: Load progression: add 2-10% load once you can do one or two reps more than the target number.

quotes.text: When training at a specific RM load, it is recommended that 2-10% increase in load be applied when the individual can perform the current workload for one to two repetitions over the desired number.

claims.text: Breathe out gently as the arms sweep together.

quotes.text: Exhale gently and slowly squeeze your chest muscles

plate.viewWhy: Census view is front (CFLY template, census 4a9fd86), so the plate is drawn from the front; the inward sweep from head-height handles to the hands meeting below the chest (c1, c5) and the handles crossing past each other (c8) read from the front. The card first chose side, because the frequent fault, leaning forward (c7), needs it: "The two things that define this exercise read from the side: the path from head-height handles down to below the chest (c1, c5), and the top fault, leaning forward, which ACE says happens frequently (c7)." Under LR-31 the census view decides drawable, so the lean stays the top fault with drawable false.
plate.equipment: Two cable columns (or a crossover station) with single handles set at about the top of the head (c1). Floor line.
plate.start: Standing upright in a staggered stance (c1), abs braced (c2); arms up and out to the sides with the hands no further back than the armpits (c4), elbows slightly bent, wrists straight (c3).
plate.end: Hands meet in front of the body below chest level (c5), elbows still slightly bent (c3), trunk still upright (c1, c7).

checkpoints.label: Trunk upright
checkpoints.what: The trunk stays vertical, no leaning toward the hands.

checkpoints.label: Soft elbows
checkpoints.what: A slight, fixed bend in the elbows the whole time.

checkpoints.label: Below chest
checkpoints.what: The hands meet below chest level.

mistake.what: Hands crossing past each other at the front, after the arms opened back behind the torso.
mistake.why: ACE names leaning forward as the frequent fault (c7), but a lean shows only from the side and this plate is the census front view. The next fault, arms behind the torso and the handles crossed past the midline, carries "a risk of injury in the shoulder during hyperextension and of the hand when the handles pass so close to each other" (c8, a bent-forward cable crossover tip applied by inference); ACE's decline fly page also keeps the hands from moving back past the armpits (c4).
mistake.rankNote: No source measures how often each fault happens. LR-31 step 1: leaning forward (c7). ACE's "Avoid the tendency to lean forward during this exercise as this increases the stresses within the shoulder joint, which happens frequently when the resistance used is too heavy." (c7) says the lean happens frequently, a frequency word for this fault of this exercise. No other fault passes step 1. Set aside: ACE's chest-study page is about other exercises: "In addition, many people descend too fast and let their elbows travel upward too much on the ascent, which can cause shoulder injury." and "What many people miss in this motion is the natural arc" (the barbell bench press), "Many users will adopt their own technique on this machine to do more weight, which is a big mistake and can result in injury" and "Quite often, the lifter will use too much weight and be unable to complete the full range of motion or will lift the upper back off the back pad to finish the motion." (the pec deck), "which one of the most common strength-training exercises is the most effective way" and "nine of the most commonly used exercises for strengthening the chest muscles" (the study); Rabello's "commonly used exercises and their variations" (c11) is about exercises. drawable false: the lean is a still sign but shows only from the side, and the census view is front (viewWhy). plate.mistake names the next fault by the same steps. Step 2: the bent-forward cable crossover tip "While this extreme range of motion may feel good, it does little in terms of muscular conditioning, and there is a risk of injury in the shoulder during hyperextension and of the hand when the handles pass so close to each other." (c8, WEAK, applied by inference) ties the arms behind the torso and the crossed handles (handlingMistakes[1]) to harm; no other named fault is tied to harm. If that crossover tip is set aside as another exercise (as cable_fly sets aside the dumbbell fly), step 3 gives the same fault: no source has a common-mistakes list, and the arms going back too far is the fault the most read sources tell the lifter to avoid (ACE decline fly, "do not allow your hands to move past the midline of your body (level of your armpit).", c4; the crossover tip, c8), against one for the arched low back ("attempt to avoid any arching of your low back throughout the exercise", c2). The front view shows the handles crossing past the midline. Pick changed: plate.mistake moves from the lean to the crossed handles, drawable false; handlingMistakes[0] stays the lean; plate.view now follows the census (front).

tempo.text: Up 2 and down 2 rest on ACSM's 1-2 s (c12, WEAK; LR-15). Pause 1 is the pause right after the sweep, where the hands meet: ACE's "Pause momentarily then slowly return to your starting position" (c5, c12) gives no seconds, so the 1 s is a drawing convention (c12, WEAK; LR-33).

setup.step: Set both handles at about the top of your head.
A handle in each hand. Staggered stance, trunk upright.
Brace your abs and keep your low back from arching.
Pick a weight you can move without leaning forward.

posture.point: Trunk stays vertical, no leaning toward the hands.
Elbows keep the same slight bend.
Wrists straight, in line with the forearms.
Hands go no further back than the armpits.
Sweep down first, then in, in a wide arc.

handlingMistakes.fix: Lower the weight and stand tall.
Stop at the armpits going back. Let the hands just meet.
Keep the trunk still and let the arms move.

rows.means: The chest is doing the work.
Leaning forward raises stress in the shoulder joint.
rows.fix: Lower the weight and stand tall.

risks.risk: Leaning forward raises the stress in the shoulder joint.
Arms behind the body or crossing handles risks the shoulder and the hands.

zooms.right: Trunk vertical as the hands meet below the chest.
zooms.wrong: Trunk tipped forward toward the hands.

zooms.right: On the way back, hands stop level with the armpits.
zooms.wrong: Arms drawn back behind the torso.
